name: Board of Directors Fees for Family (C-Corp)

advisor.summary: A C corporation — or an S corporation, with thinner economics — that pays reasonable directors' fees to adult family members who genuinely govern deducts the fees under §162(a) and shifts that income from the entity and its high-bracket owner to lower-bracket relatives. Rev. Rul. 72-86 disciplines the whole play: directors' fees are self-employment income, so the recipient owes SE tax on top of income tax, and the arbitrage clears that roughly 14.1% drag only when the spread between the owner's rate and the recipient's is wide. In the C-corp setting the deduction also pulls earnings out ahead of the 21% corporate layer and the eventual dividend tax — which is where the strategy earns its keep. The exposure is equally plain: fees to relatives who never see a board packet get recharacterized as constructive dividends or disallowed outright. This is a governance structure first and a tax strategy second, and it is advisory because the recipients' returns sit outside the modeled household.
mechanics: The entity deducts directors' fees under §162(a) only to the extent they are ordinary, necessary, and reasonable for governance services actually rendered — benchmark per-meeting or annual-retainer amounts against what comparable closely held companies pay outside directors, and keep the comparables in the file.

Fees are non-employee compensation reported on Form 1099-NEC, and under Rev. Rul. 72-86 they are self-employment income to the director under §1402(a) — the recipient files Schedule SE, so compute the net family benefit after a roughly 14.1% effective drag.

Because the fees are compensation for services, they are earned income beyond the reach of the §1(g) kiddie tax and they support IRA contributions for the recipient — but governance is an adult's job, and fees to minors are close to indefensible.

For a C-corp payor the deduction strips out the §11 21% corporate layer before those dollars ever face dividend double-tax; for an S-corp payor the fee merely shifts income off the owner's K-1, so the arbitrage is thinner and the reasonableness bar unchanged.
Substance is the entire defense: directors are elected under the bylaws, receive board materials in advance, attend, deliberate, and vote — and the minutes prove it meeting by meeting.

authority.note: The deduction standard for the fees — ordinary, necessary, and reasonable in amount for governance actually performed; excessive amounts paid to shareholders' relatives are disallowed or recharacterized.
Directors' fees are self-employment income — the ruling that forces net-of-SE-tax math for every recipient.
Defines the SE income base, which sweeps in the trade or business of serving as a director.
The 21% corporate rate — the entity-level layer a deductible fee strips out ahead of dividend double-tax in the C-corp setting.
The kiddie tax reaches only unearned income — fees for genuine board service are earned income taxed at the recipient's own rates.
Director fees of $600 or more are reported as non-employee compensation, never as W-2 wages.

requirements: A functioning board: bylaws providing for directors, elections documented in the corporate record book, and meetings that actually happen.
Adult family directors with genuine capacity to contribute — people who read the financials and vote, not names on a signature line.
Fees set by board resolution before payment, benchmarked against comparable small-company director pay, with the comparables retained.
Minutes, agendas, distributed board packages, and timely Form 1099-NEC reporting for every paid director.
risks: Recharacterization is the leading audit theory: fees to shareholders' relatives that outrun the services are treated as constructive dividends in a C corp — no deduction, income still taxed to the family — or disallowed under §162(a) reasonableness, with the Rev. Rul. 72-86 SE tax already sunk on the recipient side.

The SE tax drag erodes the arbitrage — a fee moved from a 37% owner to a 22%-bracket adult child nets far less than the bracket spread suggests once roughly 14.1% self-employment tax is layered on; run the math for each recipient before recommending.
A paper board is fatal: no minutes, no materials, and no votes means no services, and the examiner's path to full disallowance plus accuracy-related penalties is short.
Fees well above small-company norms invite a reasonableness challenge even where the board is real — the benchmark file is the defense.
Recipients take on Schedule SE and quarterly-estimate obligations; their compliance cost belongs in the net-benefit calculation.
stateNotes: Missouri conforms through its federal-AGI starting point (RSMo §143.121): the payor's deduction and the recipient's fee income both flow into the Missouri returns without adjustment.

PTET interaction: for an S-corp payor, director fees are an entity deduction that shrinks the base on which a Missouri pass-through entity tax election is computed (SALT Parity Act, RSMo §143.436); a C-corp payor has no PTET interaction.
Fees paid to family directors living outside Missouri for board service performed here are Missouri-source income — nonresident recipients may acquire a Missouri filing obligation.
reviewChecklist: Bylaws, director elections, and the corporate record book confirm each paid family member actually holds a board seat.
Fee levels are supported by retained comparables and set by a resolution dated before payment.
Per-recipient net-benefit math sits in the file — owner's marginal rate against the recipient's bracket plus SE tax — and still favors the fee.
Minutes and distributed board materials exist for every meeting tied to a paid fee.
Forms 1099-NEC are issued, and each recipient is advised on Schedule SE and quarterly estimates.

client.teaser: Pay family members fairly for real board work — and shift that income to their lower tax rates.
client.headline: Put your family board to work — and let the company pay them for it
plainEnglish: Every corporation has a board of directors. The board reviews the numbers, weighs big decisions, and votes. Companies normally pay directors for that work, and the payment is a business expense the company deducts.

If adult members of your family truly serve on your board, the company can pay them a fair fee. The company gets the deduction. The income lands with family members whose tax rates are usually much lower than yours.

Two honest notes. The person who receives the fee owes self-employment tax on it, and we count that cost before we recommend anything. And the board work must be real — actual meetings, actual minutes, and fees in line with what small companies pay.
client.analogy: Companies pay outside advisors all the time. This pays the advisors who already care most about the business — your own family — and the tax bill shrinks with the move.
benefits: A business deduction for the company at fair, documented fee levels
Income shifts to family members in lower brackets
The fees count as earned income, so they can fund IRAs for the recipients
The next generation learns the business from inside the boardroom
steps: WE formalize the board — elections, bylaws, and the record book.
WE benchmark fair fee levels and draft the resolution before anyone is paid.
YOU hold real board meetings and keep the short minutes we template.
WE issue the year-end tax forms and brief each family director on their filing.
clientCommitments: Hold the meetings for real — the minutes must describe something that happened
Keep fees at the levels we set together, not a dollar more
Make sure each paid director reads the materials and votes

annualMaintenance: Refresh the director-fee comparables and re-set fees by resolution each year
Verify that minutes and board materials exist for every meeting tied to a fee
Issue Forms 1099-NEC each January and re-run the per-recipient net-benefit math
deliverables: Board resolutions and election documents for each family director
Director-fee benchmark memo with retained comparables
Agenda and minutes templates for the board calendar
Year-end 1099-NEC package with recipient filing guidance

suggest.reason: Real advisory work by family members can earn reasonable, documented fees.
